label: L12a
title: Optimal design of experiments: randomization vs optimization
brief: Lecture 12a argues that for small experiments, assigning subjects to groups by mixed-integer optimization beats pure randomization. Randomized groups show large covariate discrepancies (0.66 SD for four groups of ten mice), which shrink only like $1/\sqrt k$. The MIO approach standardizes covariates, then splits $n=mk$ subjects into $m$ groups of $k$ to minimize the worst pairwise gap in means plus $\rho$ times the gap in second moments, and finally randomizes which group gets which treatment. Optimized discrepancies fall exponentially in $k$: for $\epsilon=0.01$, 5 subjects per group versus 12,833 under randomization. Unbiasedness is kept because treatment labels are still randomized; inference uses a bootstrap test that re-optimizes on resampled covariates. Expect questions on the formulation and its linearization, variable counts, the discrepancy rates and sample-size table, bias, the bootstrap p-value, and statistical power.
kp: Randomization: four groups of ten mice ⇒ 0.66 SD average max pairwise discrepancy (0.47 SD with 20 per group); often larger than the treatment effect.
Discrepancy grows with the number of groups and shrinks with group size; 0.1 SD needs over 400 per group, 0.01 SD over 40,000.
MIO: standardize $w_i'=(w_i-\hat\mu)/\hat\sigma$, assign to minimize discrepancy, then randomize which group gets which treatment.
Linearize with $d$ and four constraints per pair $p<q$; $\sum_ix_{ip}=k$, $\sum_px_{ip}=1$, symmetry breaking $x_{ip}=0$ for $i<p$.
Size: $m(1+2n-m)/2$ binaries and 1 continuous; $r$ covariates add $1+m(m-1)r(r+3)/4$ continuous variables. $n=40$, $m=4$ solves in under 20 s.
Theory: $\mathbb E[Z_2^{rand}]=2\sigma/\sqrt{\pi k}$ (normal) vs median $Z_2^{opt}\le C/2^{2k}$: an exponential reduction.
Subjects per group for $\epsilon=0.01$ ($m=2$, $\rho=0$): Opt 5, Rand 12,833, Pair 65, Re-rand 83; $k^{Rand}=\lceil4/(\pi\epsilon^2)\rceil$.
Bias: optimization is mechanical (no investigator bias); randomizing treatment labels keeps the effect estimate unbiased.
Bootstrap test: $p=\frac{1}{1+B}\big(1+\sum_b\mathbb I[|\delta_b|\ge|\delta|]\big)$, reject if $p\le\alpha$; optimization gives far higher power at small $k$.

topics.x: Randomly formed groups differ substantially in pre-treatment covariates when groups are small: 0.66 SD for four groups of ten. Discrepancy rises with the number of groups and falls slowly with group size, so driving it below 0.1 SD needs over 400 subjects per group.

Standardize the covariate, then choose binary $x_{ip}$ to minimize the maximum over group pairs of the mean gap plus $\rho$ times the second-moment gap. An epigraph variable $d$ with four linear constraints per pair removes the max and absolute values; assignment, group-size and symmetry-breaking constraints complete the MIO. Treatments are randomized over the resulting groups.

With $r$ covariates, auxiliary variables $M_{pqs}$ bound the mean gap of each covariate and $V_{pqss'}$ bound the gaps in second moments and cross-moments. $d$ is at least the sum of the $M$ terms plus $\rho$ times the $V$ terms (off-diagonal terms counted twice).

Under randomization the expected mean discrepancy is order $1/\sqrt k$; under optimization it decays exponentially in $k$. For four groups of ten, 0.0005 SD vs 0.66 SD, and the subjects needed for a target $\epsilon$ are orders of magnitude fewer. Gains in higher moments that are not targeted are modest.

Being mechanical, optimization guards against investigator bias in forming groups. Randomization balances any one factor only in large samples and cannot remove hidden-factor imbalance in small ones. Because treatment identities are randomized after grouping, the observed difference stays an unbiased estimator.

To test the null of no treatment effect, compare the observed group difference $\delta$ with differences $\delta_b$ from re-optimized assignments on bootstrap resamples, giving $p=(1+\sum_b\mathbb I[|\delta_b|\ge|\delta|])/(1+B)$. In the Gomp-ex tumor simulation, optimized groups estimate the effect tightly and detect a 50 mg effect with power near 1 by about $k=10$, while randomization stays low.

Optimized groups are exponentially more similar, especially with small groups, high variability and many groups. Each extra subject per group roughly halves the discrepancy, which buys statistical power with small samples; the method also protects against bias at least as well as randomization and is feasible online.

quiz.q: Under randomization, what is the average maximal pairwise discrepancy for four groups of ten mice?
quiz.e: 0.66 SD. 0.47 is for groups of twenty; 0.0005 is the optimized value.

quiz.q: How does the randomization discrepancy behave?
o: Increases with the number of groups, decreases with group size
Decreases with both the number of groups and group size
Increases with both the number of groups and group size
Depends only on group size, not on the number of groups
quiz.e: More groups means more pairs that can be far apart; larger groups average out noise.

quiz.q: In the MIO approach, what is randomized after the optimization?
o: The order in which responses are measured
quiz.e: Groups are built by optimization, then treatment labels are assigned to groups at random.

quiz.q: What does the constraint $\sum_{i=1}^nx_{ip}=k$ enforce?
o: Every subject is assigned to exactly $k$ groups
The $k$-th subject is assigned to group $p$
quiz.e: The sum runs over subjects for a fixed group. $\sum_px_{ip}=1$ is the one-group-per-subject constraint.

quiz.q: How does optimization guard against investigator bias?
o: It is a mechanical process for forming groups
It uses more subjects per group than randomization
It hides covariates from the investigator
It matches subjects on the measured outcome
quiz.e: Groups come from a fixed optimization problem, so the investigator cannot steer group composition.

quiz.q: In the bootstrap test, the null of no effect is rejected at significance $\alpha$ when:
quiz.e: Standard rule: a small p-value means the observed $|\delta|$ is extreme relative to the bootstrap distribution.

quiz.q: Per the practical-significance slide, adding one subject per group under optimization:
o: Reduces the discrepancy by a factor $1/\sqrt k$
quiz.e: Optimization roughly halves the discrepancy per extra subject; diminishing returns describe randomization and pair matching.

quiz.q: Single-covariate MIO with $n=40$ subjects and $m=4$ groups: how many binary variables?
quiz.e: $m(1+2n-m)/2=4\cdot77/2=154$, i.e. $nm=160$ minus the $m(m-1)/2=6$ fixed to zero by $x_{ip}=0$ for $i<p$.

quiz.q: Why does the linearized MIO need four constraints per pair $p<q$?
o: $|a|+\rho|b|$ is the max of four linear terms with all sign combinations
One constraint is needed for each of the four groups when $m=4$
Means and variances each need an upper and a lower bound
quiz.e: $d\ge\pm(\mu_p-\mu_q)\pm\rho(\sigma_p^2-\sigma_q^2)$ gives $d\ge|a|+\rho|b|$. The count does not depend on $m$, and no products appear.

quiz.q: Covariate values $w=(1,2,3,6)$. Using the slides' preprocessing, what is $w_4'$?
quiz.e: $\hat\mu=3$, $\hat\sigma^2=(4+1+0+9)/4=3.5$, so $3/\sqrt{3.5}\approx1.60$. 1.39 divides by $n-1$; 0.86 divides by the variance instead of the SD.

quiz.q: Increasing $\rho$ in $Z_m^{opt}(\rho)$ makes the optimizer:
o: Weight second-moment gaps more relative to mean gaps
Use more groups for the same number of subjects
quiz.e: The objective is $|\mu_p-\mu_q|+\rho|\sigma_p^2-\sigma_q^2|$; $\rho=0$ is what ignores second moments.

quiz.q: Subjects per group needed for expected discrepancy at most $0.001\sigma$ ($m=2$, $\rho=0$):
quiz.e: Row $\epsilon=0.001$. 8,130 is re-randomization and 514 is pairwise matching.

quiz.q: Using $k^{Rand}=\lceil4/(\pi\epsilon^2)\rceil$, how many subjects per group does randomization need for $\epsilon=0.2$?
quiz.e: $4/(\pi\cdot0.04)\approx31.8$, rounded up to 32. 31 rounds down.

quiz.q: With normal covariates, $\mathbb E[Z_2^{rand}]=2\sigma/\sqrt{\pi k}$. To halve the expected discrepancy you must:
quiz.e: Discrepancy scales as $1/\sqrt k$, so halving it needs $4k$. Adding one subject roughly halves it under optimization, not randomization.

quiz.q: In the higher-moments table (slide 22), why is optimization's edge large in moments 1–2 but small in moments 3–5?
o: The MIO only targets the first two moments
Higher moments are always identical across groups
quiz.e: At $k=20$ the mean gap is 1.23e-6 (Opt) vs 0.258 (Rand), but the third-moment gap is 0.600 vs 0.947: untargeted moments improve only modestly.

quiz.q: What can randomization NOT guarantee when samples are relatively small?
o: An unbiased estimate of the treatment effect
quiz.e: Randomization equalizes any one factor only with large enough samples. Unbiasedness holds at any sample size.

quiz.q: In the tumor-growth example, which tests were used?
o: Bootstrap test for optimization; standard randomization test for the others
Standard randomization test for all four methods
Bootstrap test for all four methods
t-test for optimization; bootstrap test for the others
quiz.e: Optimized assignments are not random, so the method uses its own bootstrap test that re-optimizes on resampled covariates.

quiz.q: In the multiple-covariate MIO, how many continuous variables are there for $m=2$ groups and $r=2$ covariates?
quiz.e: $1+m(m-1)r(r+3)/4=1+2\cdot1\cdot2\cdot5/4=6$: one pair with 2 $M$'s, 3 $V$'s, plus $d$. 5 forgets $d$; 7 counts $r^2$ second-moment terms.

quiz.q: Bootstrap test with $B=199$; 9 resamples give $|\delta_b|\ge|\delta|$. At $\alpha=0.05$:
quiz.e: $p=(1+9)/(1+199)=0.05$ and the rule is $p\le\alpha$. 0.045 omits both +1 terms; 0.0503 adds one only to the numerator.

quiz.q: Going from $k=10$ to $k=20$ per group, how do expected discrepancies change by the slide 20 formulas ($\propto1/\sqrt k$ for Rand, $\propto2^{-k}$ for Opt)?
quiz.e: $\sqrt{10/20}\approx0.71$ and $2^{-10}\approx1/1024$. Treating the optimization rate as polynomial gives the 0.5 or 0.25 answers.

quiz.q: What does the $\delta_0=0$ panel of the power figure show, and why does it matter?
o: No method rejects much above 5%: the tests keep their size
Optimization rejects far more often: it inflates false positives
Randomization never rejects: it is too conservative to use
Rejection rises with $k$: power grows under the null
quiz.e: With no true effect, Rand, Pair and Re-rand hover around the dashed $\alpha=0.05$ line and Opt stays below it (about 0.01–0.04), so optimization's power gains are not bought with false positives.

quiz.q: Why does the formulation fix $x_{ip}=0$ for $i<p$?
o: To remove solutions that only permute group labels
To stop a subject from joining multiple groups
To make the LP relaxation integral
quiz.e: Relabeling groups leaves the objective unchanged, so many equivalent optima slow branch-and-bound. Single assignment is $\sum_px_{ip}=1$, and sizes come from $\sum_ix_{ip}=k$.

written.q: Formulate the MIO that splits $n=mk$ subjects with one covariate into $m$ groups of $k$. Define the variables, linearize the objective, explain each constraint, and count the variables.
written.m: Standardize: $w_i'=(w_i-\hat\mu)/\hat\sigma$ with $\hat\mu=\sum_iw_i/n$, $\hat\sigma^2=\sum_i(w_i-\hat\mu)^2/n$. Variables: $x_{ip}\in\{0,1\}$ (subject $i$ in group $p$); linear auxiliaries $\mu_p=\frac1k\sum_iw_i'x_{ip}$ and $\sigma_p^2=\frac1k\sum_i(w_i')^2x_{ip}$. Objective $Z_m^{opt}(\rho)=\min_x\max_{p\ne q}|\mu_p-\mu_q|+\rho|\sigma_p^2-\sigma_q^2|$. Linearize with an epigraph variable: minimize $d$ s.t. for every $p<q$, $d\ge\pm(\mu_p-\mu_q)\pm\rho(\sigma_p^2-\sigma_q^2)$ (four sign combinations, whose max equals $|a|+\rho|b|$). Constraints: $\sum_ix_{ip}=k$ (equal group sizes); $\sum_px_{ip}=1$ (each subject in one group); $x_{ip}=0$ for $i<p$ (breaks permutation symmetry among group labels). Size: $m(1+2n-m)/2$ binaries ($nm$ minus the $m(m-1)/2$ fixed zeros) and one continuous variable; $n=40$, $m=4$ solves to optimality in under 20 s. After solving, randomize which group gets which treatment.
k: Epigraph $d$ with four constraints per pair and why
Group-size, assignment and symmetry-breaking constraints explained

written.q: A lab plans four groups of ten mice. Argue for optimization over randomization, covering covariate discrepancy, required sample sizes, bias and unbiasedness, and statistical power. What are the limits of the advantage?
written.m: Discrepancy: randomization gives an average maximal pairwise discrepancy of 0.66 SD for four groups of ten (0.47 SD with twenty), often larger than the treatment effect; optimization with $\rho=0.5$ gives 0.0005 SD. Rates: $\mathbb E[Z_2^{rand}]=2\sigma/\sqrt{\pi k}$ (order $1/\sqrt k$) vs median $Z_2^{opt}\le C/2^{2k}$: exponential, and each extra subject per group roughly halves the optimized discrepancy. Sample size: for $\epsilon=0.01$, 5 subjects per group optimized vs 12,833 randomized (65 pair matching, 83 re-randomization). Bias: optimization is mechanical, so there is no investigator bias; treatment labels are randomized across the optimized groups, so the observed difference stays unbiased. Randomization cannot remove hidden-factor imbalance in small samples. Power: in the Gomp-ex simulation, optimization's estimates cluster tightly around the true effect, and a 50 mg effect is detected with probability near 1 by $k\approx10$, while randomization stays near 0.1; under no effect all tests reject at or below about 5% (optimization below). Limits: the MIO matches only the moments it targets (moments 3–5 improve modestly), hidden factors are not directly balanced, and inference needs the bootstrap test rather than the standard randomization test.
k: Investigator bias and unbiasedness via randomized labels
Power evidence and size control under the null
Limits: untargeted moments, hidden factors, special test

written.q: Describe the bootstrap hypothesis test for an optimized two-group design and compute the p-value when $B=99$ and 3 bootstrap differences satisfy $|\delta_b|\ge|\delta|$. What do you conclude at $\alpha=0.05$?
written.m: Null: every subject would have had the same response under either treatment. Steps: (1) find an optimal assignment of the $n$ subjects into two groups, randomly permuting which gets which treatment; (2) administer treatments and measure responses $v_i$; (3) compute $\delta=\frac1k\sum_{\text{group 1}}v_i-\frac1k\sum_{\text{group 2}}v_i$; (4) for $b=1,\dots,B$, draw a bootstrap sample of the covariates with replacement, re-solve the optimal assignment (with random permutation), and compute $\delta_b$ from the corresponding responses; (5) $p=\frac1{1+B}(1+\sum_b\mathbb I[|\delta_b|\ge|\delta|])$; (6) reject if $p\le\alpha$. Here $p=(1+3)/(1+99)=0.04\le0.05$, so we reject the null of no effect. The re-optimization step is needed because the assignment is not random, so the standard randomization test's reference distribution does not apply.
k: Observed $\delta$ as a difference of group means
Resample covariates and re-optimize for each $b$
